questions.moduleTitle: Foundations: Base Models and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: Before training Composer 2, the team evaluated several potential open-source base models including GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and DeepSeek V3.2. Three base model evaluations contributed to the selection process: coding knowledge measured with FreshBench, state tracking measured with an internal benchmark similar to LoCoDiff, and codebase perplexity measured using their private monorepo. The team intentionally did not consider coding agent benchmarks when testing base models, as agentic and long-horizon capabilities can drastically change during the RL stage. Based on these evaluations and additional considerations such as efficiency in infrastructure, they selected Kimi K2.5 as the base model for Composer 2.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 aims to improve the language model's base knowledge in the domain of coding. This stage is divided into three distinct phases. The bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length, followed by a shorter long-context extension phase to 256k sequence length. Finally, there is a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks. Training was performed in MXFP8 on NVIDIA B300s using the AdamW optimizer.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage aims to improve the language model's base knowledge, specifically in the domain of coding. This approach extends the base model with a continued pretraining stage on a large code-dominated data mix. The purpose of this stage is to provide a base model for the subsequent agentic RL training by specializing the model on coding knowledge and capabilities. While the team starts with base models naturally trained with large amounts of code data, they find that additional supervised learning reliably improves knowledge benchmarks and leads to improved coding performance of the final coding agent.

questions.lessonContent: Similar to prior work, Composer 2 uses Kullback-Leibler divergence for regularization in its reinforcement learning training. Many open-source implementations estimate KL using the estimator k3 = (r − 1) − log r, which is an unbiased estimator that reduces variance when the sampling policy and training policy are close. However, Amini et al. demonstrates that the variance of the k3 estimator increases drastically as the two distributions diverge. The k2 estimator does not suffer from variance blow-up but is biased. Due to the variance issues with k3 for diverging policies, Composer 2 instead uses the standard estimator k1 = −log r for KL divergence estimation. This choice provides more reliable estimates during training when policy divergence occurs.

questions.lessonContent: When implementing policy gradient algorithms for Composer 2, the team followed findings from Dr. GRPO research regarding gradient bias minimization. A key decision was to remove the length standardization term from GRPO because it introduces a length bias into the training process. Additionally, the team does not normalize group advantages by their standard deviation, as doing so results in a degenerate case where small behavioral differences get massively upweighted within groups where every rollout achieves equal correctness. These modifications help minimize the bias that can arise from transforming the underlying advantage in policy gradient methods. The team operates in the single-epoch regime where the same prompt is never trained on twice.

questions.lessonContent: The reinforcement learning infrastructure for Composer 2 is designed with a decoupled service architecture to enable larger-scale global training, high availability, and independent scaling and sharding. The RL infrastructure consists of four decoupled services that work together: training, environments, inference, and evaluations. This decoupling naturally makes training more resilient to failures in these services, and during training runs, the system observed many cases where services had partial or full outages without failing the training job. The production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute, demonstrating the scalability enabled by this architectural approach. Each service can scale and be sharded independently based on workload requirements.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 optimizes its training infrastructure by adopting Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary scaling axis for long contexts. Previous stacks relied on Tensor Parallelism (TP), which creates less efficient skinny local matrix multiplications. In contrast, CP improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions in projections. Additionally, CP requires less communication than TP, reducing the overhead associated with scaling to longer sequence lengths.

questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 training infrastructure uses a novel variant of NVFP4 quantization for the Mixture-of-Experts forward pass to ensure stability. The standard NVFP4 format uses FP32 per-tensor scales, which the team found to be fragile. This fragility arises because per-tensor scaling makes training batch-variant, leading to collapsed numerical precision, and causes inter-token scale values to leak future token information into past tokens, resulting in biased gradients. Consequently, the implementation uses FP32 per-token scales instead to avoid these issues.

It makes training batch-variant and leaks future token information into past tokens.
It increases the communication overhead during the all-gather of latent vectors.
